item.title: LXC and Linux System Containers
item.description:
LXC is a userspace interface for Linux containment features. It combines the liblxc library, command-line tools, and distribution templates to create system containers: isolated Linux userspaces that share the host’s kernel.

An LXC container can boot an init system, run several services, maintain persistent package state, and expose virtual network interfaces. The operating model therefore resembles a lightweight Linux machine more than an OCI application container. LXC remains a container runtime, however, because it does not boot a guest kernel or emulate hardware.

item.title: Quay Container Registry
item.description:
Quay is a container-image registry product from Red Hat. It stores and distributes OCI and Docker-compatible images, with organization and repository access controls, robot accounts, vulnerability scanning integrations, and optional repository mirroring. A registry is not a source-control system: image tags identify published artifacts, while source and build definitions should remain in version control.

item.title: Linux GUI Applications in Containers
item.description:
Containers do not automatically have access to the host display session. A GUI client needs the appropriate display socket, environment variables, and credentials; exposing them grants the container meaningful control over the user session and should be done only for trusted images.

X11 #

For X11, mount the host socket directory—typically /tmp/.X11-unix—and pass DISPLAY. The client also needs the matching Xauthority cookie, usually supplied by mounting a narrowly scoped cookie file and setting XAUTHORITY. Do not use xhost +; it disables access control for the display. X11Docker can create a more constrained wrapper around this setup.

item.title: VNC Ecosystem
item.description:
VNC transports a remote framebuffer and input events using the Remote Framebuffer protocol. It is useful for isolated graphical desktops, browser-delivered sessions, and container workloads that should not receive the host’s display socket.

Servers and Virtual Displays #

Xvfb is an in-memory X server with no physical display. x11vnc shares an existing X display through VNC; it does not itself create a virtual desktop. Other VNC servers, such as TigerVNC’s Xvnc, combine an X server with a VNC endpoint. noVNC is a WebSocket-to-VNC client that lets a browser connect through a compatible proxy.

item.title: Docker-in-Docker
item.description:
Docker-in-Docker (DinD) runs a Docker daemon inside a container. It is sometimes useful for disposable CI jobs that must build or test images, but it adds privileged-kernel access, nested storage, and caching complexity. It is not the default choice for every job that invokes docker.

Choose the Right Build Model #

There are three common models:

  1. DinD: a dedicated daemon runs in the job network namespace. It provides separation from the host daemon but commonly needs privileged mode.
  2. Docker-outside-of-Docker: the job mounts the host Docker socket. It is simple and fast, but any process that can use the socket can control the host Docker daemon.
  3. Daemonless builders: BuildKit, Kaniko, Buildah, or a managed builder create OCI images without exposing a general-purpose host daemon.

Use the least privileged option that supports the build. Rootless BuildKit or a remote BuildKit builder can preserve cache efficiency without granting a CI job access to the runner’s Docker socket.

item.title: Docker Fundamentals
item.description:
Docker, the container system that still depends on your kernel, your CPU ISA, and its x86-64 syscall. An application that runs in a docker container is said to be containerized.

Component Overview #

Docker Engine: dockerd #

dockerd is a CLI daemon program that manages installed containers on the local system. It is branded as Docker Engine or Docker CE (Community Edition), and is open-source and free.

The dockerd daemon listens on the UNIX domain socket /var/run/docker.sock for incoming clients. This socket file must be readable by the user who runs a docker client to establish the socket (to send HTTP request). If you installed the Docker Engine from your Linux distro’s package manager, this socket file may be only readable by the root or a special user group dedicated to Docker, e.g. docker. You may choose to add yourself to that user group, or simply become root whenever using the docker client. Use docker info to check if the dockerd is running and the client has permissions.
